cities.d: the booming capital and largest city by far, fastest growing city in Africa, with a good claim to be the music capital of West Africa.

hidden.d: Dates to 1907 (although current cathedral built in 1925) after a Catholic mission nearby was relocated here.
Reopened in mid-2013 after complete renovation. Fewer than 200 animals from more than 100 species. Nice lion exhibit.
Very fitting with a dove perched atop a world cupped in an equilateral triangle.
If you try really hard, it kind of looks like the tower in Astana.
Houses caves with rock paintings, and offers good views across the city.
This is a rather remarkable looking monument to the independence of Mali, complete with a minaret on top. But watch out for heavy traffic in the area.

x.intro: Bamako is the capital of Mali and straddles the Niger River. With a population of around 2.5 million in 2020, it's the largest city in Mali and one of the largest in West Africa.

must.d: Portraits and items related to women and Malian life.

n.de: Musée de la Femme Muso Kunda
n.es: Museo de la Mujer Muso Kunda
n.fr: musée de la Femme Muso Kunda

must.d: The tallest building in Mali (20 floors high), with Neo-Sudanic architecture and features reminiscent of the Sudan-Sahelian architecture of mosques in Djenne and Timbuktu. A readily visible landmark on the Bamako skyline.

n.ar: برج بي سي إي إيه أو (باماكو)

x.safe: In Bamako you have a high chance of encountering the police. You should always at least carry a copy of your passport and visa. It is often not sufficient to just show your driving license and this might lead to a ride to the police office - if you're not prepared to bribe your way out. Notice that the police often stops taxis.

cities.d: small city on the Niger in the far east of the country, one time capital of the Songhai Empire, and home to the Tomb of Askia.

hidden.d: A giant sand dune across the river from Gao, named for its glowing pink color at sunrise and sunset. Best reached by pirogue. The top has beautiful views of the surrounding landscape, especially after the rainy season.

x.intro: Gao is a city of 90,000 inhabitants in the Gao region of Mali.

must.d: Constructed in 1495 by Songhai emperor Askia Mohamed Toure, the Askia Tomb (known locally as the Askia Mosque) is a mud-brick pyramid designed to look like the Great Pyramids of Egypt, which Mohamed saw on his pilgrimage to…

x.safe: Information on the security situation can be found in the warning box at the top of the Mali page.

cities.d: Mali's westernmost big city, by the border with Senegal, and best known for being the hottest continuously inhabited location in Africa.

hidden.d: Site of a major battle between the Toucouleur Empire and French colonizers. The fort still stands and is open to the public.

x.intro: Kayes is a city in the Kayes Region on the river Senegal in the West African country of Mali.

cities.d: a city across three islands in the middle of the Niger; gateway to Dogon Country.

x.around: The centre of Mopti is compact enough that you should be able to walk everywhere. Taxis are, however, available.

hidden.d: While not quite as impressive as other brick mosques across Mali it is still a sight to behold, the mosque is generally not open to non-Muslims. It has been inscribed on the tentative List UNESCO World Heritage sites since 2009.

x.intro: Mopti is one of the main ports in Mali, and a good gateway for many of the country's most impressive attractions such as Djenné, Timbuktu, and Dogon Country.
x.safe: Mopti is full of people who want to sell you souvenirs and tours to various places, including river trips. Many are extremely persistent and will not take no for an answer; getting rid of them is something which you will get better at with time.

cities.d: Mali's third largest city and one-time capital of the Bamana Empire.

x.around: You can easily walk around the centre of the town, but to reach some of the outlying hotels you can easily get a taxi ~250-500cfa.

hidden.d: Completed in 2009, this large mosque is the main gathering point for Friday prayers and an impressive sight.

cities.d: Mali's second largest city and one-time capital of the Kénédougou Empire.

hidden.d: Located in the city centre, the Mamelon hill used to be a sacred site of the Kénédougou kings. Now a French colonial tower stand at the site.

x.intro: Sikasso is a city in Sikasso Region in the south of Mali, 375 km (233 mi) from the capital Bamako. It is the second largest city in Mali with about 230,000 inhabitants.

cities.d: the legendary Saharan city of gold, trans-Saharan trade, and Islamic scholarship is nowadays a (fairly commercialized) centre of Tuareg culture.

x.around: There are taxis, camels and donkeys, and not much more, but you can easily walk from one end of the city to the other in under an hour. All the mosques are in the old town, which can be walked across in just a few minutes.

hidden.d: German explorer Heinrich Barth made an incredible five-year journey across Sahara and reached Timbuktu in 1853. This tiny museum containing reproductions of Barth's drawings and extracts of his writings.
Has an interesting mix of artifacts and contemporary folk art, albeit the museum feels a bit dusty. Some artifacts have however been stolen in the recent civil war.
Alexander Gordon Laing (1794–1826) was the first European to reach Timbuktu, but was murdered shortly after his departure.
Commemorates the ceremonial burning of 3000 weapons in March 1996, in honor of the end of the Tuareg rebellion. Many of the old guns are embedded in cement at the base of the monument.

x.intro: Timbuktu (also Tombouctou or Timbuctu) is a Tuareg city on the Niger River in the country of Mali. Its long history as a trading outpost that linked black Africa below the Sahara Desert with Berber and Islamic traders throughout north Africa, and thereby indirectly with traders from Europe, has given it a fabled status. Combined with its relative inaccessibility, "Timbuktu" has come to be used as a metaphor for exotic, distant lands. Timbuktu is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

must.d: Has an impressive minaret and is worth a visit. The mosque doubles as an madrasah, an Islamic learning centre.
Built in 1327 and is the largest and most impressive of the three mosques. There's an army barracks just to the south of the mosque, taking photos with caution is recommended.
Built in 1400 AD, the mosque is a prime example of the earthen architecture of the Sudano-Sahelian style. It was partly destroyed in 2012 but has since been reconstructed.

n.es: Mezquita y Mausoleo de Sidi Yahya

intro: A landlocked country in the Sahel, Mali remains one of the poorest countries in the world, but it has wonderful musicians and some incredible sights, including four UNESCO World Heritage sites and the historic city of Timbuktu.

other.d: a sandstone plateau in the Sahara home to rock paintings, salt mines operated for centuries, and a surprising array of wildlife.

x.intro: The Adrar des Ifoghas is a large plateau in the eastern Kidal region of Mali covering roughly 250,000 km². Adrar is the Tamasheq word for mountain while Ifoghas is the name of a Tuareg clan which lives in the region, the French so named it to differentiate from their (long-held) Adrar in Mauritania. The area is home to a surprising number of animals, including gazelles, antelopes, hyenas, jackals, snakes, & lizards.

next.d: the closest thing to a city anywhere near the Adrar.

x.safe: Do not underestimate the remoteness! You must have proper supplies for an extended trip into the desert, about a week is necessary to travel from Kidal and spend a few days exploring. Bring two weeks' worth of supplies in case you get lost or caught in a dust storm. Independent travel is highly discouraged and a guide and 4x4 is absolutely essential.

other.d: a trek through this landscape of scattered cliff-side villages is not to be missed by any Mali visitor. The famous Bandiagara Escarpment is a World Heritage Site

x.around: There are almost no roads in the region, except those connecting a couple of towns used as base camps with the neighboring regions. You will need to go on foot and be in relatively good shape. A number of the hikes are quite strenuous, although you'll see village women trekking up them with piles of goods on their heads.
x.intro: Dogon Country (French: Pays Dogon) is the name used for a region of south-central Mali renowned for its secluded villages embedded on cliffs that are up to 500 m tall which were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1989. These are near the city of Bandiagara.

next.d: It is the nearest large town with all the supplies people could need as well as good connections back to Bamako.

x.safe: If trekking, you should be in good physical shape and carry and drink lots of water to prevent dehydration. Head covering is also recommended as the midday sun is exceedingly strong and can even catch a well-hydrated traveler offguard. Good, sturdy shoes, whether general running/walking type or hiking boots are recommended for the treks as the terrain can be difficult to traverse on some of them.

other.d: once a religious and commercial centre to rival Timbuktu, this small town of multi-storey mud buildings is quite a sight. It has declared a World Heritage site by UNESCO.

x.around: For traveling short distances walking may be the best method as it allows you to appreciate the scenery and look at the mud based architecture in the city.
x.intro: Djenné is a city in Mali, famous for its mosque, which is the biggest mudbrick building in the world. As of 1987, the city had a population of 12,000. Djenné has been recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. UNESCO says on its website that "Djenné became a market centre and an important link in the trans-Saharan gold trade."

must.d: This is the main tourist attraction in the city. It is what made the city a UNESCO heritage site.
